newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai markets dismiss modest CPI jump, focus on '97.
newsitem.headline: Thai markets dismiss modest CPI jump, focus on '97.

text.p: Investors in Thai financial markets on Tuesday dismissed a modest rise in November inflation, focusing instead on the prospect of dwindling price pressures over 1997.

Commerce Ministry data showed the consumer price index (CPI) up 4.8 percent year-on-year in November, in-line with market forecasts and compared with October's 4.3 percent gain. Month-on-month November CPI rose 0.5 percent.

"Market sentiment is very poor at present. The inflation figures released by the commerce ministry earlier today were in line with earlier expectations and didn't help the market," said First Asia Securities investment analyst Virat Tippanontakul.
"The mood is so poor that even the recent reduction of interest rates by several major banks failed to have some positive reaction to the market," he said.
For calendar 1996, economists expect an average annual inflation rate of between 5.7 and 5.8 percent, virtually unchanged from 1995 when inflation averaged 5.8 percent.

Traders said fears over a broader economic slowdown are weighing on local financial markets, driving the benchmark SET share market index down 1.6 percent on Tuesday -- the fourth straight loss in the index.
The SET shed 14.82 points on Tuesday to finish at 905.81.
"Thailand's slow economic growth was the key factor forcing investors, including foreigners, to sell shares today," said Somchai Trairattanapirom of Sitca Investment and Securities.
But analysts said the economic slowdown should cut into consumer spending and help subdue inflation pressures over 1997.
"Next year we expect the inflation rate to be at about 5.0 percent due mainly to the slowing economy," said Arporn Chewakrengkai, chief economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Analysts said the expected fall in inflation growth next year could give the central bank room to ease interest rates. The interbank rate climbed as high as 13.50 percent in mid-November, but has since fallen to around 8.50-9.00 percent.
"With the improved outlook for inflation next year, interest rates will continue their declining trend," Seamico Securities said in a report.
New Commerce Minister Narongchai Akrasanee attributed the high November annual inflation rate to rises in non-food prices, especially those of cigarettes and alcoholic beverages.
Analysts said a recent excise tax hike on cigarettes and alcohol had caused the sharp price jump. Prices of food and beverages, however, were flat in November over October.
Narongchai said the average inflation rate in the first 11 months stood at 5.9 percent. He did not give a comparative figure for the same period last year.
